content: Alendronate is a medication prescribed to treat and prevent osteoporosis, a condition characterized by weakened and brittle bones that are prone to fractures. It is commonly used in postmenopausal women, as well as in men and women who are taking corticosteroids, which can increase the risk of osteoporosis. Additionally, alendronate is used to treat Paget's disease of bone, a disorder where bones become soft, weak, deformed, and prone to fractures. Alendronate belongs to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates, which work by inhibiting bone breakdown and increasing bone density. Alendronate is available in tablet and liquid forms, both of which are taken orally. The liquid form is typically taken once a week on an empty stomach in the morning. The 5-mg and 10-mg tablets are usually taken daily on an empty stomach in the morning, while the 30-mg and 70-mg tablets are taken once a week under the same conditions. For Paget's disease, the 40-mg tablets are taken daily for six months. It is crucial to follow the exact instructions provided by your doctor or pharmacist. Taking alendronate incorrectly can reduce its effectiveness and may cause damage to the esophagus or mouth. It should never be taken at bedtime or before getting out of bed. Tablets must be swallowed whole with a full glass (6–8 ounces) of plain water, and the liquid form should be followed by at least 2 ounces of plain water. Avoid taking alendronate with any liquids other than plain water, such as tea, coffee, juice, milk, or sparkling water. Do not chew, crush, or suck on the tablets. After taking alendronate, refrain from eating, drinking, or taking other medications (including vitamins or antacids) for at least 30 minutes. Additionally, remain upright (sitting or standing) for at least 30 minutes after taking the medication and until you have eaten your first meal of the day. Alendronate is not a cure for osteoporosis or Paget's disease but helps manage these conditions as long as it is taken regularly. It may take three months or longer to observe an increase in bone density. Do not stop taking alendronate without consulting your doctor, even if you feel well. Before starting alendronate, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it or any of its ingredients. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as some may interact with alendronate. Notify your doctor if you have difficulty sitting or standing upright for 30 minutes, a history of low blood calcium levels, esophageal problems, or any other medical conditions such as anemia, swallowing difficulties, ulcers, cancer, infections, dental issues, or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss this with your doctor, as alendronate can remain in the body for years after discontinuation. Alendronate may cause serious jaw problems, particularly if you undergo dental surgery or treatment while taking the medication. A dental examination and necessary treatments should be completed before starting alendronate. Maintain good oral hygiene and consult your doctor before any dental procedures while on this medication. Alendronate can also cause severe damage to the mouth, esophagus, or stomach if not taken as directed. If you experience symptoms such as new or worsening heartburn, difficulty swallowing, pain when swallowing, or chest pain, stop taking alendronate and contact your doctor immediately. To support bone health, your doctor may recommend lifestyle changes such as avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol consumption, engaging in weight-bearing exercises, and consuming a diet rich in calcium and vitamin D. If dietary intake is insufficient, your doctor may suggest supplements. If you miss a daily dose of alendronate, skip it and take the next dose the following morning. For weekly doses, take the missed dose the morning after you remember, then resume your regular schedule. Never take more than one dose in a single day or double up on doses to compensate for a missed one. Alendronate may cause side effects. Common side effects include nausea, stomach pain, constipation, diarrhea, gas, bloating, changes in taste, bone or joint pain, headache, dizziness, and flu-like symptoms. Severe side effects include new or worsening heartburn, difficulty swallowing, chest pain, bloody vomit, black or tarry stools, fever, skin reactions, swelling, difficulty breathing, jaw pain, or dental issues. If you experience any severe symptoms, stop taking alendronate and contact your doctor immediately. Store alendronate in its original container, tightly sealed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom or freeze the liquid form. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of an overdose, give the affected person a full glass of milk and contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the person collapses or stops breathing, call 911. Do not induce vomiting or allow the person to lie down. Symptoms of overdose may include heartburn, nausea, stomach pain, bloody vomit, difficulty swallowing, or black, tarry stools. Keep all medical and laboratory appointments while taking alendronate, as your doctor may order tests to monitor your response to the medication. Do not share this medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refills. Alendronate is sold under the brand names Fosamax® and Fosamax Plus D®.
